title: Using Self-Reported Training Characteristics to Better Understand Who Is More Likely to Sustain Running-Related Injuries Than Others: The Garmin-RUNSAFE Running Health Study
authors: Abrahamson J, Lindman I, Eriksen MB, Kibsgaard A, Nielsen RO
journal: Scandinavian Journal of Medicine & Science in Sports
population: Adults (18+) tracking running with a Garmin watch, 18 months of Garmin Connect data and weekly injury questionnaires; baseline self-reported experience, frequency, greatest weekly distance and programme use
findings: 7,391 runners; cumulative injury proportion 57.8% (95% CI 56.4-59.2) after 1000 km of running.
Those with few (<1 year) or many (>40 years) of years of running experience had the most RRIs.
Fewest new RRIs for runners with a self-reported weekly distance above 105 km (cRD -31.6, 95% CI -23.1 to -40.1) and running 7 times per week (cRD -47.1, 95% CI -35.9 to -58.3).

More RRIs with lower weekly frequency (<2 runs per week), shorter weekly distance (<25 km) or no structured running programme in the conclusion; the abstract's structured-programme estimate (cRD 4.4, 95% CI 0.9-7.8) is positive yet is described as the fewest-RRI group, so the sign is internally inconsistent.
limitations: Abstract-level verification only. Baseline self-report, analysis at a fixed 1000 km, possible confounding by exposure (high-volume runners may be those who tolerate training), structured-programme sign unclear in the abstract. A descriptive risk-group paper, not a test of progression or session spikes.
implications: Fewer than 1 year of experience carries the highest risk among experience groups: consistent with a more conservative regime for new runners, though the study cannot give step size.
Very experienced runners (more than 40 years) also had more RRIs, probably an age or experience signal; do not loosen limits automatically for long running history.

Low frequency (under 2 runs per week) and low weekly distance (under 25 km) mark higher injury risk; a plan could treat a runner as new or returning when logged frequency is that low, whatever they report as experience (a design choice).

verification.notes: Re-fetched Crossref (first author Abrahamson, 5 authors, online 2024-12-23) and Europe PMC abstract (PMID 39713859, pubYear 2025). Corrected: the abstract's methods name 'greatest running distance in 1 week' and self-reported weekly distance as the baseline exposure, so the >105 km finding is reworded; the structured-programme sign inconsistency is stated plainly; the 'survivor' remark is demoted to 'possible'. Relevant to novice versus experienced rule differences only, not to thresholds.
